content:
Hello! I'd like to present a basic foundation for Newtonian point-particle mechanics I've been developing in a fork. It seems a natural fit for the classical mechanics section of Physlib.

There are three layers and a proof of concept:

  • Particles and forces (ParticleMechanics/Basic.lean): a Particle is a position function together with its mass. Force is a vector function together with the particle it targets, and InternalForce just extends Force with a "source" particle
  • Systems (ParticleMechanics/System.lean): a System bundles a frame of reference, finite set of particles, internal and external forces, and Newton's laws. On top of this sit aggregate quantities: center of mass, total momentum, kinetic energy.
  • Frames of reference (ReferenceFrame.lean): a time-dependent origin and basis in Space. Motivation: physlib's Space conflates two different things, absolute affine space (no origin, no preferred axes) and a coordinate vector space in which positions get components. The tension is evident at Space/Basic.lean:65. My formalization of reference frames makes the separation type-level. Each inertial frame carries its own type frame.Vector of coordinate vectors, which are convertible to Space and back using the frame's origin and basis. This is expressed using only the affine structure imported from Space/Basic.lean

Proof of concept (Pendulum/Defs.lean, Pendulum.lean): the simple pendulum formalized as a two particle System (pivot and bob, tension as the internal force, gravity and support as external forces). The equation of motion θ'' = −(g/L) sin θ is then derived from those raw particle and force constraints

Happy to hear comments before I carve this into PRs (frame layer, particle/force layer, system layer, maybe pendulum).

Very excited to see reference frames :). Just a quick look, I would expect that InertialReferenceFrame to be a prop rather then a definition, and velocity to be a derived quantity. Easy changes, but I think they would make that file a lot better!

How does your notion of a pendulum relate to my naive notion of a point mass under the force of gravity restricted to live on a circle.

InertialReferenceFrame extends ReferenceFrame, so it carries the same data. Therefore it can't be a mere prop. The velocity field actually refers to displacement per unit time, and since Space uses EuclideanSpace for displacements and the existing formalization of Time assumes an implicit unit, velocity should also just be EuclideanSpace.

The pendulum system includes a bob particle that is the point mass under the force of gravity restricted to live on a circle.

One could define it something like the following I think: 

structure IsInertial (d : ℕ)  (f : ReferenceFrame d) : Prop where
  /-- Elapsed time times `velocity` is exactly the origin's displacement. -/
  origin_moves_uniformly : ∃ v,
    ∀ t₁ t₂, toReferenceFrame.origin t₂ -ᵥ toReferenceFrame.origin t₁ = (t₂ - t₁).val • v
  /-- The coordinate axes neither rotate nor change scale with time. -/
  basis_conserved : ∀ t₁ t₂, toReferenceFrame.basis t₁ = toReferenceFrame.basis t₂

The problem with making velocity a new bit of data is that you loose proof-irrelevance.
That would be elegant. Moreover InertialReferenceFrame could then be defined as the subtype {frame : ReferenceFrame // frame.IsInertial}

Yep, this seems like a good idea! Though it may actually be easier just to carry around the prop 

{frame : ReferenceFrame} (h : frame.IsInertial)

But this is a design choice, and people have different opinions about it.
Thanks. I created a PR based on the feedback: https://github.com/leanprover-community/physlib/pull/1519
